Topic 01 — The Warm-Up

The Case for Warming Up

  • Force ↑ Rate of force development, reaction time, and force output at higher velocities
  • Oxygen Bohr effect → higher temp releases more O₂ from hemoglobin/myoglobin
  • Blood Flow ↑ Blood flow to active muscles via vasodilation
  • Metabolism Faster ATP turnover, especially in anaerobic pathways
  • Mindset ↑ Psychological preparedness for performance
80%+ of published research shows warm-up improves performance.
Topic 01 — The Warm-Up

Two Families of Effects

Temperature-Related
↑ Muscle & core temperature.
Enhanced neural function.
Disruption of transient connective tissue bonds.
Non-Temperature-Related
↑ Blood flow to muscles.
↑ Baseline oxygen consumption.
Postactivation potentiation.
Active warm-ups (movement-based) beat passive (external heating) — they drive both effect families plus activity-specific metabolic pathways.
Topic 01 — The Warm-Up

No Single Perfect Warm-Up

Injury Risk
Evidence is unclear, but likely positive.
↑ Muscle temp → ↑ resistance to muscle tears.
Specificity Required
Structure & content must reflect activity, athlete, and logistics.
Many effective warm-ups exist — there's no single prescription.
Plan the warm-up around the activity, required physiological responses, the athlete, and logistics.
Topic 02

Components
of a
Warm-Up

Topic 02 — Components of a Warm-Up

Four Progressive Processes

An effective warm-up builds progressively through four processes.

1
Stimulate
Cardiorespiratory & metabolic processes
2
Raise Temperature
Body & working-muscle temperature
3
Increase ROM
Relative to the upcoming activity
4
Increase Intensity
Muscle contraction intensity, progressively
Topic 02 — Components of a Warm-Up

The Traditional Two-Phase Structure

General Warm-Up
~5 min low-intensity aerobic activity (jog, skip, cycle).
↑ Heart rate, blood flow, deep muscle temp.
↓ Viscosity of joint fluids.
Specific Warm-Up
Movements matching the sport's biomechanical patterns.
Includes rehearsing the skills to be performed.
Static stretching used to follow the general phase — dynamic stretching has mostly replaced it.
Topic 02 — Components of a Warm-Up

Numbers You Must Know

10–20 min
Typical total warm-up duration.
≤ 15 min
Warm-up should end within this window before the activity — benefits fade after that.
~5 min
Typical general (low-intensity) warm-up phase.
Topic 03

Targeted &
Structured
Warm-Ups

Topic 03 — RAMP Protocol

Competition vs. Training Warm-Up

Competition Warm-Up
Focused entirely on maximizing short-term performance.
Training Warm-Up
Optimizes acute performance and builds short-, medium-, and long-term development.
Athletes spend a lot of training time warming up. Planned well, that time builds real development — not just readiness.
Video: CSCS Prep
Topic 03 — RAMP Protocol

The Three Phases of RAMP

Raise
Elevate physiological parameters.
Simultaneously build sport-skill patterns.
Activate & Mobilize
Develop movement competency.
Squat, lunge, and other key patterns.
Potentiate
Progressive intensity up to competition/session level.
RAMP builds on general/specific structure but explicitly targets short-, medium-, and long-term performance.
Topic 03 — RAMP Protocol · Raise

Raise — More Than Just Aerobic Activity

Looks Like General Warm-Up
↑ Body temp, heart rate, respiration, blood flow.
↓ Joint fluid viscosity.
But the Focus Differs
Not generic aerobic drills — activities that simulate upcoming movement patterns.
Builds skill capacity from the very first minute.
Topic 03 — RAMP Protocol · Activate & Mobilize

Mobility, Not Static Flexibility

Flexibility = static range of motion. Mobility = moving freely and effectively — combining motor control, stability, and flexibility.
  • Goal Develop athlete's movement competency, not lengthen muscles
  • Method Build the phase around key patterns (squat, lunge, etc.)
  • Timescale Longer-term consideration, not just next-session readiness
Topic 03 — RAMP Protocol · Activate & Mobilize

Static Stretching in Warm-Up — The Debate

The Concern
Can reduce force, power, running speed, and strength endurance.
Linked to ↓ musculotendinous stiffness / ↓ neural drive.
The Nuance
Short-duration static stretching (< 60 s) shows no detrimental effect.
Follow it with intense activity to offset any decrement.
Sports needing greater ROM (gymnastics, martial arts) may still benefit — weigh it with a benefit-risk analysis.
Topic 03 — RAMP Protocol · Potentiate

Potentiate — The Missing Phase

Progressive intensity → Treppe (staircase) effect → Motor neuron more sensitive to input → Muscle activated with less neural drive
Most critical for sports needing high speed, strength, or power — yet often omitted from traditional warm-ups.
  • Use Sport- or capacity-specific activities (e.g. speed & agility)
  • Progression Staged increase in intensity up to competition/session demand

Preparatory

Topic 04 — CNS Preparatory Exercises

What Is PAPE?

Postactivation performance enhancement (PAPE): a low-volume acute stimulus that briefly boosts neuromuscular performance afterward.
  • Premise Prior high-intensity activity can enhance motor unit recruitment & rate coding
  • Modalities Resistance training, resisted/assisted sprinting, isometrics, plyometrics
  • Outcome Most research shows effects on subsequent sprint and/or jump performance
Topic 04 — CNS Preparatory Exercises

Potentiation vs. Fatigue

Activities that generate the most potentiation also tend to generate the most fatigue — the fitness-fatigue balance.
Highly Individual
Response depends on stimulus type, intensity, volume, and timing.
Logistically Hard
Equipment and time constraints often rule out effective team-wide use.
Topic 04 — CNS Preparatory Exercises

Sample Preconditioning Combinations

Lower Body
Back squat (60–90% 1RM) → countermovement jump.
Resisted sprint (10–60% BW) → sprint.
Depth jump → countermovement jump.
Upper Body
Bench press (60–90% 1RM) → medicine ball throw.
Push press (40–80% 1RM) → shot put.
Rest before the potentiated activity: 1–12 minutes, adjusted to the athlete and session goals.
Topic 04 — CNS Preparatory Exercises

Guidelines & Precautions

  • Training Level Well-trained, high speed/power athletes respond best
  • Trade-Off Resistance protocols → greatest gain but also greatest fatigue
  • Accessibility Plyometrics & resisted sprints — lower potential, more usable in warm-ups
  • Transfer The closer the preconditioning activity is to the main activity, the greater the transfer
  • Decision Base use on a comprehensive cost-benefit analysis
Topic 05

Flexibility

Topic 05 — Flexibility

Static vs. Dynamic Flexibility

Static Flexibility
ROM about a joint during a passive movement.
No voluntary muscular activity — external force does the work.
Dynamic Flexibility
Available ROM during active movement.
Requires voluntary muscular action; generally > static ROM.
A normal ROM cannot guarantee normal movement — static flexibility does not directly transfer to sport performance.
Topic 05 — Flexibility

Optimal, Not Maximal

The most flexible athlete is not always the most successful — the goal is optimal, sport-specific flexibility.
  • Mobility Integrates balance, postural control, and perception through ROM
  • Both Extremes Risky Inflexibility AND hyperflexibility can increase injury risk
  • Force Over ROM Greater ROM can extend the time force is applied → ↑ impulse
Topic 05 — Flexibility

Factors Affecting Flexibility

Fixed by Biology
Joint structure (ball-and-socket > ellipsoidal > hinge).
Age & sex — younger and female athletes tend more flexible.
Tissue & Neural
Muscle, MTU, tendons, ligaments, fascia, skin.
Stretch tolerance & neural control (afferent/efferent).
Trainable
Resistance training through full ROM.
Activity level — stretching & full-ROM training maintain flexibility.
Topic 05 — Flexibility

Elasticity, Plasticity & Muscle Bulk

Elasticity
Returns to original resting length after a passive stretch.
Plasticity
Assumes a new, greater length after a passive stretch — the target of stretching.
A significant ↑ in muscle bulk can impede joint ROM (e.g. large biceps/deltoids limiting triceps stretch) — a trade-off for power athletes.
Topic 05 — Flexibility

The Stretch Reflex

Rapid stretch → Muscle spindle fires → Sensory neuron → Motor neuron in spine → Reflexive contraction of stretched muscle
Static stretching moves too slowly to trigger the reflex → muscle relaxes → greater stretch. Ballistic/dynamic stretching moves fast enough to trigger it → limits ROM.
Topic 06

Types of
Stretching

Topic 06 — Types of Stretching

Three Broad Categories

Stretching techniques fall into three broad categories.

1
Static
Slow movement, held end position
2
Dynamic
Active, controlled movement through ROM
3
Precontraction (PNF)
Muscle actions before a passive stretch
Topic 06 — Types of Stretching · Static

Static Stretching

Active
Athlete's own muscles supply the force to reach end position.
Passive
A partner or machine supplies the external force.
Hold end position 10–30 seconds. Too slow to trigger the stretch reflex → lower injury risk than ballistic stretching, easy to learn, effective at ↑ ROM.
Topic 06 — Types of Stretching · Dynamic

Dynamic Stretching

  • Definition Controlled, moderate-paced active motion through a large ROM
  • Specificity Mimics the sport movement — e.g. walking knee lift mimics a sprinter's knee drive
  • Muscle State Muscle stays active through the ROM (unlike static, which relaxes)
  • Trade-Off Ideal for warm-up, but may be less effective than static/PNF for building static ROM
Topic 06 — Types of Stretching · Dynamic

Ballistic Stretching

A special type of dynamic stretch — uses intense bouncing movements to reach end ROM, rather than controlled motion.
Dynamic
Controlled, avoids bouncing.
Smaller ROM, but full active control throughout.
Ballistic
Triggers the stretch reflex → can limit ROM.
Higher injury risk, especially with prior injury history.
Topic 06 — Types of Stretching · PNF

Proprioceptive Neuromuscular Facilitation

Autogenic Inhibition
Active contraction of a muscle stimulates its own GTO.
→ Reflexive relaxation of that same muscle during the next stretch.
Reciprocal Inhibition
Contracting the opposing (agonist) muscle stimulates its GTO.
→ Simultaneous reflexive relaxation of the stretched (antagonist) muscle.
Topic 06 — Types of Stretching · PNF

Three PNF Techniques

Hold-Relax
Prestretch (10s) → isometric hold (6s) → passive stretch (30s).
Gain via autogenic inhibition.
Contract-Relax
Prestretch (10s) → concentric action through full ROM → passive stretch (30s).
Gain via autogenic inhibition.
Hold-Relax + Agonist Contraction
Same first two phases as hold-relax.
Athlete then concentrically contracts the agonist into the new ROM.

Topic 06 — Types of Stretching · PNF

The Most Effective Technique

Hold-relax with agonist contraction produces the greatest ROM gain — it stacks reciprocal inhibition (primary) and autogenic inhibition (secondary).

Topic 06 — Types of Stretching · PNF

Guidelines & Precautions

  • Contraction Moderate intensity, sustained 6–10 s
  • Stretch Passive stretch duration ~30 s
  • Volume 2–4 repetitions, 30 s rest between reps
  • Prep Ensure a thorough general warm-up beforehand
  • Communication Clear communication with partner is essential — especially for smaller joints
Topic 06 — Types of Stretching

Programming Considerations

15–30 s
Recommended static stretch duration; diminishing returns beyond ~30 s.
2–8 weeks
Short-term intervention window for measurable flexibility gains.
1x/week
PNF may be the exception — one session per week may be optimal.
Frequency (sessions/week) seems to matter more than single-session duration — total daily stretch time may matter as much as any one stretch.
Topic 06 — Types of Stretching

When to Stretch

Post-Practice
Within 5–10 min after practice, while muscles are warm.
↑ Collagen elasticity from residual heat; effect on soreness is mixed.
Separate Session
Precede with a thorough general warm-up.
Useful as a recovery-day session after competition.

15–30 s

Topic 07

Static Stretch
Catalog

Topic 07 — Static Stretch Catalog · Neck

Look Right and Left

1
Stand or sit with the head and neck upright.
2
Turn the head to the right using a submaximal concentric muscle action.
3
Turn the head to the left using a submaximal concentric muscle action.
Muscles affected: Sternocleidomastoid
Topic 07 — Static Stretch Catalog · Neck

Flexion and Extension

1
Standing or sitting with head and neck upright, flex the neck by tucking the chin toward the chest.
2
If the chin touches the chest, try to touch the chin lower on the chest.
3
Extend the neck, coming as close as possible to touching the head to the back.
Muscles affected: Sternocleidomastoid, suboccipitals, splenae
Topic 07 — Static Stretch Catalog · Shoulders and Chest

Straight Arms Behind Back

1
Standing, place both arms behind the back.
2
Interlock fingers with palms facing each other.
3
Straighten the elbows fully.
4
Slowly raise the arms, keeping the elbows straight.
5
Keep the head upright and neck relaxed.
Muscles affected: Anterior deltoid, pectoralis major
Topic 07 — Static Stretch Catalog · Shoulders and Chest

Seated Lean-Back

1
Sitting with legs straight and arms extended, place palms on the floor about 12 in (30 cm) behind the hips.
2
Point the fingers away from the body (backward).
3
Slide the hands backward and lean backward.
Muscles affected: Anterior deltoid, pectoralis major
Topic 07 — Static Stretch Catalog · Posterior of Upper Arm

Behind-Neck Stretch (Chicken Wing)

1
Standing or sitting, abduct the right shoulder and flex the elbow.
2
Reach the right hand down toward the left scapula.
3
Grasp the right elbow with the left hand.
4
Pull the elbow behind the head with the left hand to increase shoulder abduction.
5
Repeat on the other side.
Muscles affected: Triceps brachii, latissimus dorsi
Topic 07 — Static Stretch Catalog · Upper Back

Cross Arm in Front of Chest

1
Stand or sit with the left elbow slightly flexed (15–30°) and the arm across the body (horizontal adduction).
2
Grasp the upper arm just above the elbow, placing the right hand on the posterior side of the upper arm.
3
Pull the left arm across the chest (toward the right) with the right hand.
4
Repeat on the other side.
Muscles affected: Posterior deltoid, rhomboids, middle trapezius
Topic 07 — Static Stretch Catalog · Upper Back

Arms Straight Up Above Head (Pillar)

1
Stand with the arms in front of the torso, fingers interlocked, palms facing out.
2
Slowly straighten the arms above the head with the palms up.
3
Continue to reach upward with the hands and arms.
4
While continuing to reach upward, slowly reach slightly backward.
Muscles affected: Latissimus dorsi
Topic 07 — Static Stretch Catalog · Lower Back

Spinal Twist (Pretzel)

1
Sitting with the legs straight and upper body nearly vertical, place the right foot to the left side of the left knee.
2
Place the back of the left elbow on the right side of the right (now flexed) knee.
3
Place the right palm on the floor 12–16 in (30–41 cm) behind the hips.
4
Push the right knee to the left with the left elbow while turning the shoulders and head to the right as far as possible.
5
Repeat on the other side.
Muscles affected: Internal oblique, external oblique, piriformis, erector spinae
Topic 07 — Static Stretch Catalog · Lower Back

Semi-Leg Straddle

1
Sit with knees flexed 30–50°; let the legs totally relax.
2
Point the knees outward; the sides of the knees may or may not touch the floor.
3
Lean forward from the waist and reach forward with extended arms.
Muscles affected: Erector spinae
Topic 07 — Static Stretch Catalog · Lower Back

Cobra Stretch

1
Lie prone on the floor or mat.
2
Place the hands on the floor in a push-up position just below the shoulders, elbows flexed and close to the body.
3
Keep the legs extended with the top of the toes or feet resting on the floor.
4
Lift the head and chest while pressing down through the hands to extend the spine (arch the back).
5
Keep the pelvis and lower body in contact with the floor while looking forward.
6
Hold the position while breathing slowly and deeply.
7
Slowly lower back to the floor to return to the starting position.
Muscles affected: Rectus abdominis, pectoralis major, iliopsoas, erector spinae
Topic 07 — Static Stretch Catalog · Hips

Forward Lunge (Fencer)

1
Standing, take a long step forward with the left leg and flex the left knee until it is directly over the left foot.
2
Keep the left foot flat on the floor.
3
Keep the right knee moderately flexed.
4
Keep the back foot pointed in the same direction as the front foot.
5
Keep the torso upright and rest the hands on the hips or front leg.
6
Slowly lower the hips forward and downward.
7
Repeat on the other side.
Muscles affected: Iliopsoas, rectus femoris
Topic 07 — Static Stretch Catalog · Hips

Supine Knee Flex

1
Lie on the back with legs straight.
2
Flex the right knee and hip, bringing the thigh toward the chest.
3
Place both hands behind the thigh and continue to pull the thigh toward the chest.
4
Repeat on the other side.
Muscles affected: Hip extensors (gluteus maximus, hamstrings)
Topic 07 — Static Stretch Catalog · Hips

Figure Four Stretch

1
Lie supine on the floor.
2
Flex and externally rotate the left hip to cross the left ankle over the right thigh.
3
Flex the right hip and pull it toward the chest until a comfortable stretch is felt.
4
Hold, then release.
5
Repeat on the other side.
Muscles affected: Gluteus medius, piriformis
Topic 07 — Static Stretch Catalog · Torso

Side Bend With Straight Arms

1
Stand with feet shoulder-width apart.
2
Interlace the fingers with palms away from the torso, facing outward.
3
Reach upward with straight arms.
4
Keeping the arms straight, lean from the waist to the left side without flexing the knees.
5
Repeat on the other side.
Muscles affected: External oblique, latissimus dorsi, serratus anterior
Topic 07 — Static Stretch Catalog · Torso

Side Bend With Bent Arm

1
Stand with feet shoulder-width apart.
2
Flex the right elbow and raise it above the head.
3
Reach the right hand down toward the left shoulder.
4
Grasp the right elbow with the left hand and pull it behind the head.
5
Keeping the elbow flexed, lean from the waist to the left side without flexing the knees.
6
Repeat on the other side.
Muscles affected: External oblique, latissimus dorsi, serratus anterior, triceps brachii
Topic 07 — Static Stretch Catalog · Torso

Lunge With Spinal Twist

1
Assume a lunge position with the right leg forward.
2
Place the left hand on the floor directly parallel to the right foot.
3
Rotate the body, extending the right arm toward the ceiling, and hold.
4
Repeat on the other side.
Muscles affected: Erector spinae, semispinalis, hamstrings, gluteus maximus, iliopsoas, quadriceps, obliques, pectoralis major, anterior deltoids
Topic 07 — Static Stretch Catalog · Anterior of Thigh and Hip Flexor

Side Quadriceps Stretch

1
Lie on the right side with both legs straight.
2
Place the right forearm flat on the floor and the upper arm perpendicular to the floor.
3
Place the left forearm at a 45° angle to the torso.
4
Flex the left knee, moving the heel of the left foot toward the buttocks.
5
Grasp the front of the ankle with the left hand and pull toward the buttocks.
6
Repeat on the other side.
Muscles affected: Quadriceps, iliopsoas
Topic 07 — Static Stretch Catalog · Posterior of Thigh

Sitting Toe Touch

1
Sit with the upper body nearly vertical and legs straight.
2
Lean forward using hip flexion and grasp the toes with each hand — or the ankles if flexibility is limited.
3
Slightly pull the toes toward the upper body and pull the chest toward the legs.
Muscles affected: Hamstrings, erector spinae, gastrocnemius
Topic 07 — Static Stretch Catalog · Posterior of Thigh

Semistraddle

1
Sit with the upper body nearly vertical and legs straight.
2
Place the sole of the right foot on the inner side of the left knee, outer right leg resting on the floor.
3
Lean forward using hip flexion, grasp the toes of the left foot with the left hand, pulling toward the upper body as the chest is pulled toward the left leg.
4
Repeat on the other side.
Muscles affected: Gastrocnemius, hamstrings, erector spinae
Topic 07 — Static Stretch Catalog · Groin

Straddle (Spread Eagle)

1
Sit with the upper body nearly vertical and legs straight; abduct the hips, spreading the legs as far as possible.
2
With both hands, grasp the toes of the left foot and pull slightly while pulling the chest toward the left leg.
3
Repeat toward the center, grasping right toes with the right hand and left toes with the left hand, pulling the torso forward and down.
Muscles affected: Gastrocnemius, hamstrings, erector spinae, hip adductors, sartorius
Topic 07 — Static Stretch Catalog · Groin

Butterfly

1
Sitting with the upper body nearly vertical and legs straight, flex both knees, bringing the soles of the feet together.
2
Pull the feet toward the body.
3
Place the hands on the feet and the elbows on the legs.
4
Pull the torso slightly forward as the elbows push down, causing hip abduction.
Muscles affected: Hip adductors, sartorius
Topic 07 — Static Stretch Catalog · Calf

Wall Stretch

1
Stand facing the wall with feet shoulder-width apart, toes about 2 ft (0.6 m) from the wall.
2
Lean forward, placing the hands on the wall.
3
Step back about 2 ft (0.6 m) with the stretch leg while flexing the opposite knee.
4
Extend the knee of the stretch leg and lower the heel to the floor to apply the stretch.
5
Repeat on the other side.
Muscles affected: Gastrocnemius, soleus, Achilles tendon
Topic 07 — Static Stretch Catalog · Calf

Step Stretch

1
Place the ball of one foot on the edge of a step or board 3–4 in (8–10 cm) high, other foot flat on the step.
2
With straight legs, lower the heel of the foot on the edge of the step as far as possible.
3
Repeat on the other side.
Muscles affected: Gastrocnemius, soleus, Achilles tendon
Topic 08

Dynamic Stretch
Catalog

Topic 08 — Dynamic Stretch Catalog

Arm Swings

1
Stand erect and raise the arms in front of the body until parallel to the floor.
2
While walking over a prescribed distance, swing the arms in unison to the right so the left arm crosses the chest and the right arm swings behind the body.
3
Immediately reverse direction to swing the arms in unison to the left.
4
Movement should occur only at the shoulder joints — keep the torso and head facing forward.
5
Alternate swinging the arms in unison to the right and left.
Muscles affected: Latissimus dorsi, teres major, anterior and posterior deltoids, pectoralis major
Topic 08 — Dynamic Stretch Catalog

Glute Bridge

1
Lie supine with the knees flexed to about 90°, feet hip-width apart and flat on the floor.
2
Pushing the feet into the floor and squeezing the glutes, lift the hips up toward the ceiling until the body forms a straight line.
3
Hold for a second, then return the hips to the floor.
4
The action can use a single leg as an alternative to a double leg.
Muscles affected: Gluteus maximus, hamstrings, erector spinae
Topic 08 — Dynamic Stretch Catalog

Inchworm

1
Stand erect with feet shoulder-width apart.
2
Slightly flex the knees, flex forward at the waist, and place hands shoulder-width apart flat on the floor.
3
Shift body weight back with buttocks high in the air, forming an inverted V.
4
Move the hands alternately forward in small steps until the body is in a push-up position.
5
Walk the legs to the hands using small steps, keeping the knees slightly flexed.
6
Repeat the motion over a prescribed distance.
Muscles affected: Erector spinae, gastrocnemius, gluteus maximus, hamstrings, soleus, anterior tibialis
Topic 08 — Dynamic Stretch Catalog

Quadruped Reach and Rotate

1
Assume a quadruped position.
2
Raise the left hand and extend it under the body, reaching as far to the right as possible.
3
Reverse the action, pulling the left hand back before pulling the arm back and turning the body away from the support arm.
4
Keep the lumbar spine neutral so the action occurs mainly in the thoracic spine.
5
Carry out the action in a slow, controlled manner.
6
Repeat on the other side.
Muscles affected: Obliques, erector spinae, rectus abdominis, levator scapulae, subscapularis, rhomboids, serratus anterior, subclavius, pectoralis major, pectoralis minor, latissimus dorsi, medial deltoid
Topic 08 — Dynamic Stretch Catalog

Lunge Walk

1
Stand erect with feet parallel and shoulder-width apart.
2
Take an exaggerated step forward with the left leg, planting the foot flat, pointing straight ahead.
3
Allow the left hip and knee to slowly flex, keeping the left knee directly over the left foot.
4
Slightly flex the right knee and lower it to 1–2 in (3–5 cm) above the floor.
5
Keep the torso perpendicular to the floor by sitting back on the right leg.
6
Forcefully push off the floor by extending the left hip and knee.
7
Pick up the right foot and place it next to the left — do not stutter-step forward.
8
Stand erect, pause, then step forward with the right leg, progressing forward with each step.
Muscles affected: Gluteus maximus, hamstrings, iliopsoas, quadriceps
Topic 08 — Dynamic Stretch Catalog

Lateral Lunge

1
Stand with feet hip-width apart, facing forward.
2
Take a relatively large lateral step with the right foot, keeping the left foot in contact with the floor.
3
Hinge at the hips, pushing them back, and flex the left hip and knee to about 90° while the right knee stays fully extended.
4
Keep the body aligned within the base of support — do not lean forward.
5
Return to the starting position and repeat on the same leg or alternate legs.
Muscles affected: Quadriceps, hip adductors, hip abductors, gluteus maximus, gluteus medius
Topic 08 — Dynamic Stretch Catalog

Lunge Walk With Front Leg Extension

1
Take an exaggerated step forward with the right leg into a lunge stance, right knee over right foot, rear (left) knee about an inch off the floor.
2
Flex the torso forward, reaching the hands toward the right foot; from here, lift the hips up and back, extending the right knee to a near-full extension, stretching the hamstrings.
3
After holding the stretch, extend the torso to erect, step the rear (left) foot forward, and repeat on the other side.
Muscles affected: Hamstrings, gluteus maximus, iliopsoas, quadriceps
Topic 08 — Dynamic Stretch Catalog

Speed Skater Lunge

1
Assume an upright stance, feet hip-width apart, arms at the sides.
2
Shift body weight to the left foot while dropping the hips back and down, reaching the right leg behind and across to the opposite side, extending the right knee fully with a contralateral (left) arm reach.
3
Push back to the starting position and repeat on the other side.
4
For a more advanced version, initiate the movement with a lateral hop.
Muscles affected: Quadriceps, gluteus maximus, gluteus medius, hip adductors, hamstrings
Topic 08 — Dynamic Stretch Catalog

Lunge With Overhead Side Reach

1
Stand erect with feet parallel and shoulder-width apart.
2
Take an exaggerated step forward with the left leg, planting the foot flat, pointing straight ahead.
3
Allow the left hip and knee to slowly flex, keeping the left knee directly over the left foot.
4
Slightly flex the right knee and lower it to 1–2 in (3–5 cm) above the floor.
5
Reach up high with the right arm and bend the torso laterally toward the left leg.
6
Return to an erect torso, then forcefully push off the floor by extending the left hip and knee.
7
Pick up the right foot and place it next to the left — progress forward with each step.
Muscles affected: Gluteus maximus, hamstrings, iliopsoas, latissimus dorsi, internal and external oblique, rectus femoris
Topic 08 — Dynamic Stretch Catalog

Walking Knee Lift

1
Stand erect with feet parallel and shoulder-width apart.
2
Step forward with the left leg and flex the right hip and knee to bring the right thigh toward the chest.
3
Grasp the front of the right knee or shin, using the arms to pull the knee further up and squeeze the thigh to the chest.
4
Dorsiflex the left foot as the right hip and knee flex.
5
Keeping the torso erect, pause, then step down with the right leg.
6
Shift weight to the right leg and repeat with the left leg, progressing forward with increasing ROM and speed.
Muscles affected: Gluteus maximus, iliopsoas, quadriceps, hamstrings
Topic 08 — Dynamic Stretch Catalog

Forward Lunge With Elbow to Instep

1
Stand erect with feet parallel and shoulder-width apart.
2
Take an exaggerated step forward with the left leg, planting the foot flat, pointing straight ahead.
3
Allow the left hip and knee to slowly flex, keeping the left knee directly over the left foot.
4
Slightly flex the right knee and lower it to 1–2 in (3–5 cm) above the floor.
5
Lean forward, bringing the left elbow to touch the instep of the left foot; the right hand may rest on the floor for balance.
6
Lean back to erect, then forcefully push off the floor by extending the left hip and knee.
7
Pick up the right foot and place it next to the left, progressing forward with each step.
Muscles affected: Biceps femoris, erector spinae, gastrocnemius, gluteus maximus, hamstrings, iliopsoas, latissimus dorsi, internal and external oblique, quadriceps, soleus
Topic 08 — Dynamic Stretch Catalog

Heel-to-Toe Walk

1
Stand erect with feet parallel and shoulder-width apart.
2
Take a small step forward with the right leg, placing the heel down first, then continue to dorsiflex the foot.
3
Immediately roll forward and rise as high as possible onto the ball of the right foot.
4
Swing the left leg forward to take another small step.
5
Repeat with the left leg, progressing forward with each step.
Muscles affected: Gastrocnemius, soleus, anterior tibialis
Topic 08 — Dynamic Stretch Catalog

Walking Over and Under

1
Stand erect with feet parallel and shoulder-width apart.
2
Flex the left hip and knee, abducting the left thigh until parallel to the floor.
3
Step laterally over the first hurdle with the left foot.
4
Place the left foot down, shift weight to the left leg, then lift the right leg over the first hurdle.
5
Stand erect, pause, then flex the hips and knees and dorsiflex the ankles into a full squat position.
6
Extend the left leg laterally, as if performing a lateral lunge.
7
Keeping the body weight low, move laterally, ducking under the second hurdle.
8
Stand erect, pause, and repeat in the opposite direction.
Muscles affected: Hip abductors, hip adductors, gastrocnemius, gluteus maximus, hamstrings, iliopsoas, rectus femoris, soleus
Topic 08 — Dynamic Stretch Catalog

Inverted Hamstring Stretch

1
Stand tall and take a small step forward with the left leg.
2
Flex at the waist.
3
Reach forward with the left arm and simultaneously reach back with the right leg, keeping the hips square.
4
Reach a position where a hamstring stretch is felt, eventually aiming for the body parallel to the floor.
5
Reach the right hand down toward the floor.
6
Return to the start by actively using the hamstrings and glutes of the planted leg.
7
Step forward and repeat on the other side.
Muscles affected: Gluteus maximus, hamstrings, hip abductors, hip adductors, erector spinae
Topic 08 — Dynamic Stretch Catalog

Straight-Leg March

1
Assume a tall standing position with both arms outstretched in front of the chest.
2
Rise onto the toes of the left leg while, using a straight-leg action, raising the right leg forward and up through as large a ROM as possible.
3
Once the highest point is reached, actively pull the leg back to the starting position.
4
Maintain the tall standing posture throughout.
5
Repeat on alternate legs while moving forward.
Muscles affected: Gluteus maximus, hamstrings, iliopsoas, rectus femoris
Topic 08 — Dynamic Stretch Catalog

Bear Crawl

1
Assume a push-up position.
2
Reach forward with the right arm and left leg, moving the body forward in a crawling motion.
3
Reach forward with the opposite leg and hand combination.
4
Keep the knees 1–2 in (3–5 cm) off the ground.
5
Repeat rhythmically for the desired distance or repetitions.
6
As competency increases, the ROM can increase; the crawl can also be performed backward.
Muscles affected: Erector spinae, gastrocnemius, gluteus maximus, deltoids, iliopsoas, latissimus dorsi, internal and external oblique, quadriceps
Topic 08 — Dynamic Stretch Catalog

Spiderman Crawl

1
Assume a push-up position with elbows flexed so the position is lower than normal.
2
Lift and externally rotate the left leg, bringing the knee forward at an angle outside the left elbow.
3
Walk the hands forward and across the body.
4
As this progresses, bring the right leg forward outside the right hand and repeat for the given distance.
5
Repeat, alternating sides, for the required distance.
Muscles affected: Biceps femoris, erector spinae, gastrocnemius, gluteus maximus, hamstrings, iliopsoas, latissimus dorsi, internal and external oblique, quadriceps, soleus
Topic 09

PNF Stretch
Catalog

Topic 09 — PNF Stretch Catalog

Guidelines & Precautions

  • Plan Decide on the muscle to stretch, the ROM needed, and whether PNF is best suited
  • Communicate Talk clearly with your partner before and throughout the stretch
  • Contraction Moderate intensity, sustained 6–10 s
  • Stretch Passive stretch duration ~30 s, with 30 s rest between 2–4 repetitions
  • Prepare Ensure a thorough warm-up beforehand; progress ROM gradually
  • Caution Use moderate — not high — intensity on smaller joints such as the shoulders

Calves
Chest
Groin
Quadriceps & Hip Flexors
Shoulders
